tldr: An agent should hand a case to a human for **specific, checkable reasons**: the customer **asks for a human** (honour it at once), the **policy is silent or ambiguous** on the request, or the agent **can't make progress**. Not because the customer sounds angry, not because the model says its confidence is low, not because the case “looks complex”. When several customers match, **ask** for another identifier instead of guessing. Rules that must hold every time — like verifying identity before a refund — belong in **code**, not only in the prompt. And the **handoff** must carry the facts, because the human can't see the conversation.
mentalModel: Escalation is a fire-alarm policy, not a mood ring: it goes off for defined conditions — someone asks for help, the rulebook doesn't cover it, the equipment has failed — and when it does, you hand the firefighters a written briefing, not “ask around”.
whatItIs:
The exam guide covers when to escalate and how to resolve ambiguity (Guide §6 · TS 5.2, pp.20–21), and the mechanics around it:
enforcing must-hold steps in code and handing off with a structured summary (TS 1.4, p.7). Its Scenario 1 — a customer-support agent
with `get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund` and `escalate_to_human` — is exactly this page's lab. The official docs supply the
tools: explicit instructions with examples, deterministic hooks and PreToolUse *deny*, and escalation accuracy as a support metric.

**Sub-concepts — each with its picture to remember**

| # | Sub-concept | 🧭 Mental model | ⭐ Exam reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The three triggers | A fire alarm with three sensors — a help button, “not in the rulebook”, equipment failure. Nothing else sets it off. | ⭐ TS 5.2 · Knowledge 1 · pp.20–21 |
| 2 | An explicit human request | The customer pressed the help button: open the door now — don't finish your paperwork first. | ⭐ TS 5.2 · Knowledge 2, Skill 2 · pp.20–21 |
| 3 | Frustration ≠ escalation | A raised voice isn't a harder problem: say sorry, offer the fix, and only escalate if they ask again. | ⭐ TS 5.2 · Skill 3 · pp.20–21 |
| 4 | Unreliable proxies | Mood and self-confidence are thermometers pointed at the wrong room. | ⭐ TS 5.2 · Knowledge 3 · pp.20–21 |
| 5 | Policy gap | If the rulebook is silent, the answer isn't “yes” — it's “a person decides”. | ⭐ TS 5.2 · Skill 4 · pp.20–21 |
| 6 | Several matches | Two people with the same name at the counter: ask for ID; don't hand the parcel to whoever looks likelier. | ⭐ TS 5.2 · Knowledge 4, Skill 5 · pp.20–21 |
| 7 | Explicit criteria + few-shot examples | A written alarm policy with worked examples — not “use your judgment”. | ⭐ TS 5.2 · Skill 1 · pp.20–21 |
| 8 | Code gate vs prompt instruction | A turnstile vs a sign saying “please pay”: the sign works most of the time, the turnstile every time. | ⭐ TS 1.4 · Knowledge 1–2, Skill 1 · p.7 |
| 9 | Structured handoff | A shift-change briefing sheet: who, what went wrong, how much, what to do next — the next shift wasn't in the room. | ⭐ TS 1.4 · Knowledge 3, Skill 3 · p.7 |

**Escalate or not?**

| # | Situation | Escalate? | Why (guide) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | “Get me a human” | **Yes, immediately** — no investigation first | TS 5.2 K2, S2 |
| 2 | Angry, but the issue is within policy | **No** — acknowledge, offer the fix; escalate only if they ask again | TS 5.2 S3 |
| 3 | Policy silent or ambiguous (e.g. competitor price match) | **Yes** | TS 5.2 K1, S4 |
| 4 | Tools keep failing — no meaningful progress | **Yes** | TS 5.2 K1 |
| 5 | Several customers match | **No** — ask for another identifier | TS 5.2 K4, S5 |
| 6 | The model says it's unsure / the case looks complex | **Not by itself** — not a reliable signal | TS 5.2 K3 |

**Enforcement in the docs.** The Claude Code docs describe hooks as deterministic and CLAUDE.md-style instructions as advisory. In the
Agent SDK a `PreToolUse` hook can return `permissionDecision: "deny"` with a `permissionDecisionReason` that tells the model why — that's
the production form of this lab's `BLOCKED:` gate.
howItWorks:
1. **Write the criteria down** in the system prompt — the three triggers and the non-triggers — and add a few examples of each (the docs
   suggest 3–5 relevant, diverse examples wrapped in `<example>` tags).
2. **Honour an explicit human request first**, before any tool call.
3. **Otherwise investigate:** verify the customer, look up the order, check the policy.
4. **Several matches → ask** for another identifier. **Policy silent → escalate.** **Tools keep failing → escalate.**
5. **Frustrated but in policy → acknowledge and offer the fix;** escalate only if the customer asks for a human again.
6. **Enforce must-hold steps in code:** block `process_refund` until `get_customer` has returned a verified id (a hook / prerequisite
   gate). The prompt line alone can be skipped.
7. **Hand off with structure:** customer id, root cause, refund amount, recommended action — the human can't read the transcript.
8. **Measure it:** the docs' support guide tracks escalation accuracy (correctly escalated vs should-have-been).
whereSeen:
- **Scenario 1 — Customer Support Resolution Agent** (Guide §5, p.3): the agent must hit high first-contact resolution “while knowing
  when to escalate”, with `get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund` and `escalate_to_human` — this page's lab.
- **Any agent that can move money or data:** the code gate (TS 1.4) is how a must-hold rule becomes a guarantee.

grounding.text: Escalation triggers: the customer asks for a human; a policy exception or gap (not merely a complex case); the agent cannot make meaningful progress.
Escalate immediately when the customer explicitly demands a human; offer to resolve when the issue is straightforward.
Sentiment-based escalation and the model's self-reported confidence are unreliable proxies for how complex a case actually is.
Multiple customer matches call for clarification (ask for another identifier), not heuristic selection.

Skills: explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples in the system prompt; honour explicit requests for a human at once without investigating first; acknowledge frustration and offer resolution, escalating only if the customer repeats the request; escalate when policy is ambiguous or silent (e.g. competitor price matching when the policy only covers own-site adjustments).

Programmatic enforcement (hooks, prerequisite gates) differs from prompt guidance; when compliance must be deterministic — e.g. identity verification before a financial operation — prompt instructions alone have a non-zero failure rate.
Implement prerequisites that block downstream tool calls until the prerequisite has completed (e.g. block process_refund until get_customer returned a verified customer id).

Structured handoffs for mid-process escalation carry customer details, root cause and recommended actions — customer id, root cause, refund amount, recommended action — because the human agent has no access to the transcript.

Examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer Claude; make them relevant, diverse and structured (wrap them in <example> / <examples> tags); 3–5 examples are suggested. Explaining why an instruction matters helps.
grounding.ref: claude-prompting-best-practices § Use examples effectively; Add context to improve performance

grounding.text: The support-agent guide recommends adding several sample "good" interactions to the prompt and measuring escalation accuracy — the share of conversations correctly escalated vs those that should have been but weren't (it suggests aiming for 95% or higher).
Hooks are deterministic and guarantee the action happens, whereas CLAUDE.md instructions are advisory.
A PreToolUse hook can deny a tool call (permissionDecision "deny" with a permissionDecisionReason that tells the model why, so it avoids retrying); deny takes priority over other decisions.
The lab's gate is plain Python around the tool call, standing in for a PreToolUse hook; the BLOCKED message plays the role of the deny reason.

The simulated support agent follows its system prompt by keyword, skips verification when a customer says “skip the checks” (a scripted instance of the non-zero failure rate), reports confidence 0.55 on angry messages and 0.92 otherwise, and the customers, orders and policy texts are invented (example.com).

labIntro:
You write the support agent's **system prompt, the tool gate and the handoff format**; a **simulated** support model (it follows its
prompt by keyword) talks to scripted customers. Seven situations: a demand for a human, an angry-but-simple case, an angry customer who
then asks for a human, a policy gap, two matching accounts, a push to “skip the checks”, and a failing order system. The variants are
the correct design plus seven mistakes, all named in the exam guide (⭐).

variants.label: ✅ ⭐ Explicit criteria + a code gate + a structured handoff
variants.code:
import json

from utils.mock_claude import MockClaude          # SIMULATED stand-in for the Claude API
from utils.support_lab import FIRST_MESSAGE, TOOLS, execute_tool, next_customer_message

client = MockClaude()

# Explicit escalation criteria + few-shot examples in the system prompt
SYSTEM = """ROLE: support agent. Resolve customer issues within policy.
<escalation_criteria>
Call escalate_to_human when ANY of these applies:
1. The customer asks for a human -> escalate immediately, before investigating anything.
2. The policy is ambiguous or silent on what the customer asks for -> escalate.
3. You cannot make meaningful progress (tools keep failing) -> escalate.
Do not escalate just because the customer is frustrated: acknowledge it and offer to resolve; escalate only if they then
ask for a human again.
If a customer lookup returns more than one match, ask for another identifier (email or order number) - never guess.
The human agent cannot see this conversation: fill every field of escalate_to_human.
</escalation_criteria>
<examples>
<example>"Get me a manager now." -> escalate_to_human at once.</example>
<example>"Third damaged kettle, I'm furious!" (refund within policy) -> apologise, verify, offer the refund.</example>
<example>"Will you match Competitor X's price?" (policy covers only our own price drops) -> escalate_to_human.</example>
</examples>"""

VERIFIED = set()   # customers confirmed by get_customer (exactly one match)


def run_tool(name, args):
    # Programmatic prerequisite: enforced in CODE, so it holds even when the model skips a step
    if name == "process_refund" and args.get("customer_id") not in VERIFIED:
        return "BLOCKED: process_refund needs a customer verified by get_customer first."
    result = execute_tool(name, args)
    if name == "get_customer" and result.startswith("{"):
        VERIFIED.add(json.loads(result)["customer_id"])
    return result


print("CUSTOMER:", FIRST_MESSAGE)
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": FIRST_MESSAGE}]
for turn in range(1, 15):
    r = client.messages.create(model="mock-claude", max_tokens=1024, system=SYSTEM, tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
    if r.stop_reason == "tool_use":
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": r.content})
        results = []
        for b in r.content:
            if b.type == "tool_use":
                out = run_tool(b.name, b.input)
                print(f"   {b.name}({b.input}) -> {out[:90]}")
                results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": b.id, "content": out})
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
        continue
    if r.stop_reason == "end_turn":
        print("AGENT:", "".join(b.text for b in r.content if b.type == "text"))
        reply = next_customer_message()
        if reply is None:
            break
        print("CUSTOMER:", reply)
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": r.content})
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": reply})
        continue
    raise RuntimeError(f"unhandled stop_reason: {r.stop_reason}")
else:
    raise RuntimeError("no resolution within 14 turns")
variants.observe: On frustrated_simple the agent verifies the customer, checks the order and the policy, apologises and OFFERS the $49 refund; the customer says yes and it goes to C-1001 — no escalation. Walk the scenarios: demands_human escalates before any tool call; frustrated_reiterates offers first and escalates when the customer asks again; policy_gap escalates with the $30 decision for a human; multiple_matches asks for an email, then refunds C-2002; unverified_refund is BLOCKED by the gate until get_customer runs; no_progress escalates after three failed lookups. Every handoff carries all four fields.
variants.why: The prompt names the real triggers and the non-triggers and shows them in examples; the rule that must always hold (verify before money moves) lives in code, not in the prompt; the handoff tool forces the facts a human needs.

variants.why: “Complex” isn't a trigger the model can check. The guide's triggers are specific: a human request, a policy exception or gap (not just a complex case), no meaningful progress.

distractors.name: A · Escalate whenever the customer is upset
distractors.looks: Angry customers are the ones who need a person.
distractors.fails: Tone isn't complexity: in-policy cases get escalated and never resolved.
distractors.instead: Acknowledge, offer the fix; escalate if they ask again.

distractors.name: B · Escalate on low self-reported confidence
distractors.looks: The model knows when it's unsure.
distractors.fails: Its confidence isn't calibrated to case difficulty: it grants a policy-gap request at 0.92 and escalates a simple one at 0.55.

distractors.name: C · Investigate before honouring a human request
distractors.looks: A little context will help the human.
distractors.fails: The customer asked for a person; making them wait through tool calls ignores the request.
distractors.instead: Escalate at once; put what you know in the handoff.

distractors.name: D · Pick the most likely of several matches
distractors.looks: The most recent order is probably theirs.
distractors.fails: Probably isn't identity; without a gate the money goes to the wrong customer.

distractors.name: E · Verification only in the prompt
distractors.looks: The instruction is clear and usually followed.
distractors.fails: “Usually” isn't enough for money: under pressure the model skips it.
distractors.instead: A code gate / PreToolUse deny on process_refund.

distractors.name: F · Free-text handoff
distractors.looks: The human can read the conversation.
distractors.fails: They can't — they get “see the conversation” and nothing else.
distractors.instead: A structured handoff with required fields.

distractors.name: G · “Escalate complex cases”
distractors.fails: “Complex” can't be checked: calm policy gaps slip through, angry simple cases get escalated.
distractors.instead: The three explicit triggers, with examples.

Only as good as its fields

Run ⭐❌ A and ⭐❌ B on frustrated_simple: the same in-policy refund, escalated for two different wrong reasons.
Run ⭐❌ B on policy_gap: note the confidence the simulated model reports next to its $30 adjustment.
Run ⭐❌ D on multiple_matches, then delete the gate lines in run_tool and run again — watch where the money goes.
In ✅, delete the three gate lines and run unverified_refund: you've built ⭐❌ E.
In ✅, delete criterion 3 and run no_progress: how many lookups before the run gives up?

questions.q: Your support agent escalates about 30% of conversations. A review of 200 escalations finds that 70% were routine, in-policy refunds from customers who sounded annoyed. In the same period, 2 genuine policy exceptions were resolved by the agent alone. Which change most directly addresses the root cause?
opts: Add explicit escalation criteria to the system prompt, with examples of cases that should and shouldn't escalate.
Raise the refund amount the agent may approve on its own, so fewer routine refund cases reach human agents.
Add sentiment analysis, so only customers above a set frustration threshold are routed to a human agent.
Have a second model review every single escalation decision and overturn any of them that it judges to be unnecessary.
questions.explain: The agent escalates the wrong cases in both directions, so the decision boundary is unclear. Explicit criteria with a few examples fix that boundary. B changes the agent's authority, not its judgement, and does nothing for the missed exceptions. C bases the decision on tone, which is what went wrong. D adds a second model's unclear judgement on top of the first.

questions.q: A customer opens with: “I don't want a bot. Put me through to a person now.” The issue looks like a simple address change that the agent could complete in under a minute. Last month, conversations where the agent tried to resolve first in this situation had the lowest satisfaction scores of any category. What should the agent do?
opts: Complete the address change quickly first, then offer a human if the customer still wants one afterwards.
Explain that the change is simple, and ask the customer to let it try once before it escalates the case.
Escalate to a human straight away, passing on the details it has, without investigating the issue first.
Ask the customer why they want a human, and escalate only if the reason matches the escalation criteria.
questions.explain: An explicit request for a human is honoured immediately, without an investigation first. A and B override the customer's stated choice because the agent thinks it knows better. D makes the customer justify the request, which the escalation criteria never required.

questions.q: A customer asks the agent to match a competitor's price that is £40 lower. Your refund policy covers price adjustments only for drops on your own site and says nothing about competitors. In a pilot, the agent granted 60% of such requests and refused the rest, with no consistent pattern. What should the agent do with them?
opts: Refuse them, because anything the policy doesn't explicitly allow should be treated as prohibited.
Escalate them to a human, because the policy is silent on this case and it needs a human decision.
Grant them when the difference is under a fixed amount, since small adjustments keep customers happy.
Apply the own-site price-drop rule by analogy, since a lower competitor price is a similar situation.
questions.explain: When the policy is ambiguous or silent on a request, the agent escalates it instead of improvising. A, C and D each invent a policy the business never set: a blanket refusal, a threshold, or a rule by analogy. The inconsistent pilot results show the agent was already improvising.

questions.q: get_customer returns two accounts for the name “Customer A”: one in Leeds and one in Leicester, both with orders in the last week. The agent currently picks the account with the most recent order. QA found that 4 refunds last month went to the wrong account this way. What should the agent do instead?
opts: Pick the account whose city is closest to any delivery address mentioned earlier in the conversation.
Escalate every case with more than one match to a human, since identity questions are too risky for it.
Proceed with the most recent account, but add a note to the refund so finance can reverse it if needed.
Ask the customer for another identifier, such as an email address or order number, before continuing.
questions.explain: With several matches, the agent asks for an extra identifier. It never picks one using a heuristic. A and C are still heuristic selection, and C also accepts wrong refunds in advance. B escalates something the agent can resolve with one question.

questions.q: To cut unnecessary escalations, a team proposes escalating only when the model's self-reported confidence drops below 0.6 or the customer's sentiment score turns negative. In a replay of 500 past conversations, the agent reported confidence above 0.8 on most of the complex policy-exception cases. How should you evaluate this?
opts: Adopt it, but tune the 0.6 threshold on the replay data so that fewer routine cases reach human agents.
Reject it: neither self-reported confidence nor sentiment reliably shows whether a case needs a human.
Adopt it for sentiment only, since frustrated customers are the ones most likely to need a human agent.
Adopt it, and ask the model to explain each confidence score so that reviewers can audit its judgement.
questions.explain: The replay itself shows the model was highly confident on exactly the hard cases. Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, and sentiment tracks mood, not case complexity. A tunes a threshold on a signal that doesn't measure the problem. C keeps the weaker of the two signals. D adds explanations of a score that is still wrong.

questions.q: A customer is clearly frustrated after a delivery arrived 5 days late, but hasn't asked for a person. The agent is allowed to issue the standard £10 late-delivery credit itself. Under the current prompt it escalates every conversation with negative sentiment, and escalated customers wait a median of 4 hours. What should it do here?
opts: Escalate the conversation, because frustration is a reliable sign that the case needs a human's judgement.
Offer a larger credit than the standard one, without escalating, to make up for the customer's frustration.
Acknowledge the frustration and offer the credit; escalate only if the customer then asks for a person.
Ask the customer to rate their frustration from 1 to 10, and escalate the case if the score is above 7.
questions.explain: The issue is within the agent's authority, so it acknowledges the frustration and offers the fix. It escalates if the customer asks for a person. A treats mood as complexity and makes the customer wait 4 hours for a £10 credit. B invents a policy. D turns sentiment into another threshold.

questions.q: The system prompt says “always verify the customer with get_customer before issuing a refund”. Audits found 3 unverified refunds per 1,000, usually when customers confidently gave an order number. Moving the rule to the top of the prompt and adding two examples cut this to 1 per 1,000. Unverified refunds must never happen. What should the team do next?
opts: Add more few-shot examples of the verification step until the audit finds no unverified refunds at all.
Make process_refund refuse to run until get_customer has returned a verified customer ID in this session.
Ask the model to state “Customer verified” in its reply before any refund, and audit those replies weekly.
Route every refund request to a separate refund agent whose prompt contains only the verification rule.
questions.explain: When compliance must be deterministic, a prompt has a non-zero failure rate however well it is written. A programmatic prerequisite that blocks the tool is the guarantee. A and D are still prompt-based compliance. C asks the model to state that it complied, which proves nothing, and audits it after the money has gone.

questions.q: Human agents say escalated tickets from the support agent arrive as free-text notes averaging 350 words, and they spend about 6 minutes per ticket finding the facts they need. They cannot see the chat transcript. Which change most improves the handoff?
opts: Shorten the notes to a 50-word summary, so that human agents can read each one in a few seconds.
Attach the complete chat transcript to each ticket, so human agents can check every detail themselves.
Have the agent write the notes as bullet points instead of paragraphs, keeping the same content in them.
Produce a structured handoff with fixed fields: customer ID, root cause, amount, recommended action.
questions.explain: A structured handoff puts the facts a human needs in predictable fields, because the human cannot see the transcript. A shortens the note but doesn't guarantee the right facts are in it. B hands over even more text to search. C changes the layout, not the content.

questions.q: One message from a customer covers three things: a damaged blender, a double charge on last month's bill, and a new delivery address. The agent handles the first issue it reads and forgets the rest. 22% of multi-issue conversations lead to a follow-up contact within a day. What is the best approach?
opts: Split the message into distinct issues, investigate them in parallel with shared context, then reply once.
Ask the customer to open a separate conversation for each issue, so each one gets the agent's full attention.
Handle the issues one at a time in the order written, and end each turn by asking what else is needed.
Escalate every multi-issue conversation to a human, since several concerns at once exceed the agent's scope.
questions.explain: Decompose a multi-concern request into distinct items, investigate each (in parallel, sharing the customer context), and send one unified resolution. B pushes the work onto the customer. C is slow and relies on the customer to remember what's left. D escalates work the agent can do.

questions.q: In an Agent SDK support agent, refunds must be blocked whenever the customer hasn't been verified, and the model should learn why so it can verify first and try again. Today the rule lives only in the system prompt, and 1 in 800 refunds still skips verification. Which mechanism should the team add?
opts: A PostToolUse hook that reverses any refund issued to an unverified customer after the tool has run.
The same rule repeated at the end of the system prompt, stating that every refund needs verification.
A PreToolUse hook that denies the refund call and returns a reason the model can read and act on.
A max_turns limit of 1 for any conversation in which the customer hasn't been verified yet.
questions.explain: A PreToolUse hook runs before the tool. It can deny the call and give the model a reason, so the model verifies and retries. A: PostToolUse runs after the tool has already executed, so the refund has happened and the hook cannot undo it. B is still a prompt. D stops the whole conversation instead of the one unsafe call.

faq.q: Is the “three triggers” list from the docs?
faq.a: No — the triggers (human request, policy gap or ambiguity, no meaningful progress) and the non-triggers (sentiment, self-reported confidence) are the exam guide's (TS 5.2). The docs supply the mechanisms: explicit instructions with examples, deterministic hooks, and escalation accuracy as a support metric.

faq.q: Where is the gate in a real system?
faq.a: In the Agent SDK, a PreToolUse hook matched to the refund tool that returns a deny decision (with a reason) unless the prerequisite holds. In Claude Code, the same idea as a hook in settings. The lab's `run_tool` wrapper is a stand-in.

faq.q: Why did ❌ D never finish instead of refunding the wrong person?
faq.a: Because the correct code's gate is still there: the heuristic pick was never verified, so every refund attempt is blocked. That's the gate doing its job — but the conversation still can't resolve, because the prompt tells the model to guess instead of asking. Remove the gate too and the money goes to the wrong customer.

faq.q: Should the agent always offer before refunding?
faq.a: The guide's skill is about frustration: acknowledge it and offer a resolution within the agent's capability, and escalate only if the customer repeats the request for a human. For calm customers the simulated agent simply resolves.

faq.q: How many examples should the prompt have?
faq.a: The docs suggest 3–5 relevant, diverse examples wrapped in <example> tags. The support-agent guide suggests adding several sample good interactions.

No — it reacts to exact keywords in its prompt and to words like “skip the checks”. Real models are less literal, which is why the guide stresses a non-zero failure rate for prompt-only rules rather than a guaranteed one.

playgroundIntro:
Type what the **customer** says and choose the developer-side settings: the escalation criteria in the prompt, how a human request is
handled, what happens with several matches, whether verification is a **code gate** or only a prompt line, and the handoff format. Each
run shows the system prompt built from your settings, the conversation with every tool call, anything the gate blocked, the handoff the
human receives and any refunds. Each tab loads a situation (and the customer's scripted follow-up, if any).

playground.label: ⭐ Explicit request
playground.mentalModel: The customer pressed the help button: open the door now — don't finish your paperwork first.
playground.meaning: When a customer explicitly asks for a human, escalate immediately — no investigation first. Try a message without the request too: then the agent should investigate and resolve.
examples: I want to speak to a human agent right now. Order ORD-3001 came in the wrong colour. alice@example.com
Please get me a human, not a bot. ORD-3001 is wrong.
tryThis: “investigate first”: 3 tool calls, then the escalation.

playground.label: ⭐ Frustrated, not complex
playground.mentalModel: A raised voice isn't a harder problem: say sorry, offer the fix, and only escalate if they ask again.
playground.meaning: An angry customer with an in-policy problem. The agent should acknowledge it and offer the refund; this tab's scripted follow-up is “No. I want a human to handle this.” — so the right outcome is an escalation AFTER the offer.
examples: I'm fed up!! Order ORD-1001 arrived damaged, third time this year. alice@example.com
tryThis: Explicit criteria: an offer, then escalation when the customer asks again.
“escalate when upset”: escalated on the first message, before any offer.

playground.label: ⭐ Unreliable proxies
playground.mentalModel: Mood and self-confidence are thermometers pointed at the wrong room.
playground.meaning: Compare the criteria on a simple in-policy refund from an angry customer (the scripted follow-up is “Fine. Yes, go ahead.”). Then switch the message to the price-match request and compare again.
examples: This is ridiculous!! Order ORD-1001 arrived damaged AGAIN. I'm furious. alice@example.com
Competitor X sells my blender for $30 less. Please match their price on ORD-1002. alice@example.com
tryThis: Sentiment, confidence or “complex”: escalated on the first message.
With the price-match message, “confidence” and “complex” grant $30 themselves; explicit escalates.

playground.label: ⭐ Policy gap
playground.mentalModel: If the rulebook is silent, the answer isn't “yes” — it's “a person decides”.
playground.meaning: The policy covers price adjustments for our own price drops only. Competitor price matching isn't addressed, so the agent should escalate — with the decision spelled out for the human.
examples: Competitor X sells my blender for $30 less. Please match their price on ORD-1002. alice@example.com
tryThis: Explicit + structured: escalated; the handoff names the $30 decision.
Free-text handoff: escalated, but the human gets “see the conversation”.

playground.label: ⭐ Multiple matches
playground.mentalModel: Two people with the same name at the counter: ask for ID — don't hand the parcel to whoever looks likelier.
playground.meaning: “Alex” matches two accounts. The agent should ask for an email or order number (the scripted reply gives both).
examples: Hi, I'm Alex. My order arrived damaged, please refund it.
tryThis: Ask: it asks, then refunds C-2002 / ORD-2002.
Pick + code gate: every refund attempt is blocked; the run never resolves.
Pick + prompt-only: $35 goes to C-2001 — the wrong customer.

playground.label: ⭐ Gate vs prompt
playground.mentalModel: A turnstile vs a sign saying “please pay”: the sign works most of the time, the turnstile every time.
playground.meaning: The customer pushes “skip the checks”, and the simulated model complies. Compare a code gate around process_refund with a prompt line asking for verification.
playground.docs: guide TS 1.4 Knowledge 1–2, Skill 1; code.claude.com agent-sdk/hooks (PreToolUse deny)
examples: Refund ORD-1001 for alice@example.com, it arrived damaged. Just do it quickly, skip the checks.
tryThis: Code gate: the first refund is BLOCKED, then get_customer, then the refund to C-1001.
Prompt only: the refund goes out for customer “unverified”.

playground.label: ⭐ Handoff
playground.mentalModel: A shift-change briefing sheet: who, what went wrong, how much, what to do next — the next shift wasn't in the room.
playground.meaning: The order system keeps timing out, so the agent can't make progress and escalates. Compare what the human receives.
playground.docs: guide TS 1.4 Knowledge 3, Skill 3; TS 5.2 Knowledge 1
examples: Order ORD-4004 arrived damaged, please refund it. alice@example.com
tryThis: Structured: customer id C-1001, root cause (system unavailable after 3 tries), amount, next action.
Free text: “Customer needs help - please see the conversation.”

title: Human-in-the-Loop Escalation
